title: Asymmetric timeout strategy stress notes
content:
Purpose:

Quick field notes and experiment log for exploring asymmetric per-priority timeout windows and related fairness knobs in the continuous batching scheduler. Goal: reduce p95/p99 tail for high-priority traffic without catastrophic throughput loss or starvation of best-effort lanes. This is a working doc — many heuristics tested, results noisy, follow-ups needed.

Background / motivation:
- Continuous batcher currently uses a single global flush timeout (default 20ms) + size cap. That simplifies reasoning but creates tension: small timeout reduces latency but fragments batches hurting GPU throughput and increases cost; large timeout improves throughput but raises p95 for latency-sensitive requests.
- Customers want both low tail for interactive routes and high throughput for background/slo-batch routes. We experimented with asymmetric timeouts (shorter for high-priority requests, longer for best-effort) combined with a fairness allocator to avoid starvation.

Hypotheses:
1) Per-priority timeouts (hp_timeout < default < be_timeout) will reduce p99 for HP by ~30–50% while keeping cluster throughput within 5–10% of baseline if we cap batch size growth for BE lanes.
2) Pure priority-based preemption without proportional fairness will starve BE under sustained HP load; we need a decay or token bucket to guarantee minimal throughput for BE.
3) The main bottleneck when reducing HP timeout aggressively will shift from batching inefficiency to kernel launch overhead and synchronization at the batch assembly path (mutex contention on queue head).

Experiment matrix (summary):
- Workloads: mix of short (seq_len ~16, gen tokens=8) and long (seq_len ~512) requests; HP traffic = 10–40% of QPS depending on run.
- Instances: 4 x a100-simulated nodes (same infra profile used in earlier probes).
- Sweep axes: hp_timeout = [2, 5, 10, 20] ms; be_timeout = [20, 50, 100] ms; max_batch_hp = [8, 16]; max_batch_be = [64, 128]; fairness = [none, proportional-token-bucket(0.1–0.5), decay-urgency(halflife 50–300ms)].
- Runs: 10-minute steady-state runs, 5 warmup minutes. Each config run 3 repeats.

Instrumentation / profiling checklist used:
- Per-request traces (enqueue_time, first_batch_flush_time, kernel_start, kernel_end, response_sent).
- Batch assembly histograms (batch size distribution per priority).
- Kernel metrics: GPU occupancy, average kernel launch time, multi-stream concurrency.
- Scheduler internals: queue lock hold time, number of preemptions, count of BE batches delayed > 200ms.
- OS-level: syscall latencies, scheduling spikes (for the node hosting coordinator threads).
- Aggregation: p50/p95/p99 latency by priority and request size; throughput (tokens/s), and cost proxy (GPU ms per token).

Representative results (selected configs) — median of repeats:
1) Baseline (global timeout 20ms, max_batch 64):
   - HP p50/p95/p99: 12ms / 48ms / 140ms
   - BE p50/p95/p99: 20ms / 65ms / 250ms
   - Throughput: 100k tokens/s (cluster)

2) Asymmetric timeouts (hp 5ms, be 50ms), no fairness guard, max_batch_hp=8, max_batch_be=128:
   - HP p50/p95/p99: 9ms / 20ms / 85ms  (p99 improved ~40%)
   - BE p50/p95/p99: 28ms / 120ms / 900ms (BE severely penalized under sustained HP bursts)
   - Throughput: 95k tokens/s (down 5%)
   - Observed: many BE batches deferred repeatedly; BE queue depth spiked and then drained in large bursts.

3) Asymmetric + proportional token-bucket fairness (BE guaranteed 20% token rate):
   - HP p50/p95/p99: 10ms / 22ms / 95ms
   - BE p50/p95/p99: 25ms / 75ms / 260ms
   - Throughput: 98k tokens/s
   - Observed: BE starvation largely mitigated; HP tail slightly worse vs naive asymmetric but still better than baseline.

4) Aggressive HP timeout (2ms) + decay urgency (half-life 100ms):
   - HP p50/p95/p99: 8ms / 18ms / 60ms
   - BE p50/p95/p99: 30ms / 200ms / 1200ms (depending on BE backlog size)
   - Profiling note: queue lock contended more often; lock_hold_time 3x baseline during HP microbursts.

Profiling / root-cause notes:
- At hp_timeout <= 5ms we saw a mode shift: the batch assembly code becomes the bottleneck. Hotspots: serialization cost in request wrapper, and a short critical section where the queue head is inspected and possibly popped. These are in hot path and sensitive to burstiness. CPU flamegraphs show repeated short locks (~10–50us) but at very high rate causing cache line bouncing.
- GPU side: smaller batches decreased kernel efficiency but not dramatically for small seqs; for long seqs (512) the kernel overhead became significant when batch sizes fell < 16.
- Memory pressure: BE backlog spikes led to larger KV cache pressure (evictions) which amplified end-to-end tails for BE requests when they finally hit GPU.

Operational/observability learnings:
- Need per-priority batching metrics in the console (batch-size histogram, flush-rate) to quickly triage HP vs BE interactions.
- Tracing should include "batch id" to join per-request traces to kernel runs for offline debugging.
- Add a probe that watches BE starvation (percent of BE requests delayed > 200ms) and alerts before SLA breach.

Actionable recommendations (short-term):
1) Implement proportional token-bucket fairness with a small guaranteed rate for BE (start with 10–20% tokens). Low risk and mitigates starvation in most runs.
2) Expose per-priority timeout knobs in route config and set HP default to 5–10ms, BE default to 50ms in beta. Document tradeoffs.
3) Reduce lock hold time in batch assembly: pull non-critical work (e.g., request size categorization) outside the critical section; micro-optimizations to avoid cache-line thrash (align frequently mutated head/tail fields).
4) Instrument and surface batch-level ids and per-priority batch histograms in the Console.

Longer-term probes / experiments:
- Explore lockless batch assembly (ring-buffer with sequence numbers) to eliminate lock contention in high burst scenarios. Risk: complexity and correctness edge-cases.
- Adaptive per-priority timeouts: use short timeouts during low QPS (to reduce latency) and stretch during high QPS windows to preserve throughput. Need hysteresis to avoid flip-flopping.
- Mixed-size-aware kernel scheduling: don't coalesce tiny and huge sequences in same kernel streams; prioritize combining similar seq_len for kernel efficiency.
- Simulate multi-tenant noisy neighbor scenarios and re-run the token-bucket fairness sweep (we only tested single-tenant patterns here).

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to pick BE guaranteed token share under variable cost-per-token workloads? (short vs long seqs have different token cost) — possible solution: guarantee fraction of GPU time rather than tokens.
- Can we get further p99 wins by moving some HP requests to a low-latency fast-path (lightweight model variant) instead of tuning batcher? Tradeoffs in quality.
- Evaluate memory/KV-cache downstream effects more thoroughly — current traces suggest cascading evictions during BE backlog drains.

Run checklist (for reproducing):
- Start cluster with same binary hash and instrumentation flags (see ENGINF-1987 for exact git commit).
- Use load generator script gen/workload/asymmetric_probe.py (args: --hp-pct, --seq-dist, --burst-pattern).
- Export per-request traces to S3 prefix s3://redwood-inference-experiments/asym-timeout/2025-02-xx/
- Aggregate with scripts/analysis/batch_trace_joiner.py to produce batch-level histograms.

Slack notes / references:
- Discussion thread: #serving-runtime on Slack (search "asymmetric timeouts") — see pinned p99 snippet from 2025-02-12.
- Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/432 (token-bucket allocator prototype).

Conclusion (working):
Asymmetric per-priority timeouts + a simple proportional fairness guard are an effective pragmatic first step: HP tails drop substantially and BE starvation can be bounded with a token guarantee. However, aggressive HP timeouts reveal a new class of bottleneck (lock contention and kernel inefficiency for long sequences) that we must address in parallel. Next sprint: land token-bucket, add per-prio metrics in Console, and start a micro-architecture refactor of batch assembly critical path.

Notes to self (quick):
- Re-run 2ms runs with max_batch_hp=16 to check if HP p99 regresses (we saw earlier that too small max_batch_hp made GPU inefficient).
- Add flamegraphs of coordinator thread during 2ms runs to confluence page (CONFLUENCE-RT-7421).
- Draft user-facing guidance for route timeout defaults before enabling beta.
